title: Erdogan Says Egypt Could Join New Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan Defense Pact
summary:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Egypt could join the joint defense agreement recently signed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, describing Cairo's accession as "possible" and the pact as open to further members. In an exclusive interview with Al Jazeera, Erdogan said the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement commits signatories to taking unified steps if any one of them comes under external attack.

"This agreement has sent an important message to the world," Erdogan said. The deal, also known as the Mecca Pact, was signed last Friday by Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. It stipulates that an armed attack against any one of the three would be treated as an attack against them all—a collective-deterrence provision analysts have compared to NATO's Article 5. However, officials in Islamabad cautioned against interpreting it as a NATO equivalent or as directed at any single country.

Erdogan also addressed regional tensions, including the Strait of Hormuz, which he said should be reopened because its closure serves no one's interests. He credited Qatar with playing an important mediation role. On Gaza, he said Turkey "cannot leave Gaza alone" and that Hamas was meeting its commitments while Israel continued its war. He also expressed concern over Israeli attacks on Lebanon and said he raised the issue with President Trump during Trump's recent visit to Turkey.

On Europe, Erdogan said EU membership was no longer a priority and that Europe would be "the loser." He also said he received a promise from Trump regarding F-35 fighter jets and was waiting for it to be honored, though congressional resistance remains due to Turkey's possession of the Russian S-400 air defense system.
why_it_matters: The pact could redraw security alignments across the Middle East and South Asia at a time when oil shipping, Gaza, Lebanon, and Turkey's ties with the West are all in flux. If Egypt or other countries join, a new bloc could shift how regional conflicts and trade routes are managed.

background_read: The new agreement joins three major Muslim-majority countries—Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan—in a security arrangement that echoes Cold War-era collective defense ideas.
Recep Tayyip Erdogan (Turkey's president and dominant political figure for more than two decades) has often tried to position Turkey between Western alliances and regional partnerships.
Mohammed bin Salman (Saudi Arabia's crown prince and de facto ruler) leads the kingdom's military and foreign policy, while Shehbaz Sharif is Pakistan's prime minister.

The comparison to NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance of North American and European countries) is significant because Article 5 commits members to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.

The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, is one of the world's most important oil chokepoints; Turkey's purchase of Russia's S-400 air defense system has been a long-running source of tension with Washington because U.S. officials say the system could compromise F-35 technology and reveal its secrets.

perspectives.description: Backers like Erdogan see the Mecca Pact as a strong message of unity and deterrence. For Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, it promises coordinated defense and could attract Egypt and other states, increasing their collective leverage.

Officials in Islamabad warn that the pact is not a NATO equivalent and should not be seen as aimed at any single country. Critics worry that security blocs can provoke rival powers, escalate regional tensions, and drag members into conflicts.

Analysts compare the collective-deterrence language to NATO's Article 5, but note that the new pact lacks NATO's integrated military command and legal framework. Turkey's simultaneous talks on F-35s with Washington, its S-400 purchase from Russia, and its criticism of Israel show how it is balancing competing relationships.

The pact's future depends on whether Egypt formally accedes, how the signatories define an external attack, and how Pakistan manages the comparison to NATO. Meanwhile, Erdogan says he is waiting for Trump's F-35 promise to be honored, but U.S. congressional resistance over the S-400 system remains a major obstacle.
